subtitle: Looking back: all the pasts, and what you would have done
words.intro: In Germany you finish school with a piece of paper, the Abitur, and for the rest of your life people may ask you what you got. Maya has now lived in Germany long enough to apply for something that needs one of those.

grammar[0].blocks[0].title: The four pasts
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: A CV takes the written past, or just dates and nouns. A friend gets the Perfekt.
grammar[0].blocks[1].note: The newest comes first in most German CVs today. Sign and date at the end.
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: Everything comes back here: *als ich klein war, nachdem ich gegessen hatte, wenn ich Zeit hätte*. If you can read this page without help, you’ve done B1.
grammar[0].fact: *Fernweh* and *Heimweh* are both real, and German is unusually good at this kind of word. *Heimat* can’t be translated either: it means a place, a feeling, a childhood and, at times, a political problem. Politicians handle the word carefully.

grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Du fehlst mir
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *Du fehlst mir* means I miss you, but the person missing is the subject: you are lacking to me. It’s the dative again, right at the end of the course, on the platform, when it counts.
grammar[1].fact: German speakers have many ways of avoiding the big words. *Ich hab dich lieb* is softer than *Ich liebe dich*, for friends, parents and children. It’s what a German will say to you on a platform, and you may now reply.

document.intro: A real CV from an architect in Berlin, typed on a machine, with the last lines added by hand. It’s in the short form: dates and nouns. It’s a very German life: Abitur, university, first job. Use it as your model.
document.fact: CVs in Germany are expected to account for every year, with no gaps: six months you can’t explain will be asked about. You may leave out your photo now, but many still add one, and date and sign the page at the end.
document.tasks[0].instruction: Find it on the CV and write it.
document.tasks[2].instruction: Turn the CV’s notes into sentences, in the written past.
reading.intro: Maya has been offered a job back home, and she has three days to decide. She’s writing the CV for it at Frau Huber’s kitchen table. Frau Huber is reading it over her shoulder, with her glasses on and a red pen.
reading.fact: To become a German citizen you usually need to have lived here for some years, to speak German at B1 level, and to pass a test of 33 questions on state and society, of which you must get 17 right. You have now reached the language level.
